title: Gathering the corners
hook: many gather the four fringes of the prayer shawl before the Shema

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ahavah Rabbah, the blessing of great love. Your line was great love first. Who got warmth before correction? Today, a small gesture near the end of that same blessing. Day five hundred sixty-five.

If you've ever been in a synagogue on a weekday morning, you might have seen it without knowing what it was. Partway through the prayers, people wrapped in big striped shawls reach out, one corner at a time, and gather the long knotted fringes into one hand. Front left, front right, back left, back right. Then they hold the bundle close, often against the heart, and keep holding it. It takes a few seconds, and it's timed to one phrase in the blessing. Today, the shawl, and why the corners come together.
screen: `A STRIPED SHAWL.` → `ONE CORNER AT A TIME.` → `FOUR FRINGES IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: The shawl is a tallit, a prayer shawl. What makes it a tallit isn't the stripes or the fabric. It's the fringes, tzitzit, tied on its four corners. The Torah commands them in two places. In Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish translation: "Thou shalt make thee twisted cords upon the four corners of thy covering, wherewith thou coverest thyself." Four corners, a cord on each. Now, the gesture. Near the end of Ahavah Rabbah, the blessing asks God: bring us in peace from the four corners of the earth. The Hebrew word for corners is kanfot, the same word used for the corners of the garment. It can also mean wings. So at those words, many people gather the four fringes from the four corners of the shawl into one hand. Scattered threads, brought together, while the prayer asks for a scattered people to be brought together, echoing the prophet Isaiah's picture of gathering the dispersed from the four corners of the earth. They hold the fringes through the Shema, and in its third paragraph, where the fringes are commanded, many kiss them each time the word tzitzit is said. Who wears one differs by community. In Orthodox practice it's men, in many Ashkenazi communities from marriage and in many Sephardi communities from boyhood. In many Conservative and Reform communities, women wear one too. The tallit is usually worn for morning prayer, by daylight. And the gesture is the same everywhere it's done: four corners, one hand.
screen: `TALLIT: THE PRAYER SHAWL.` · `TZITZIT ON FOUR CORNERS.` · `KANFOT: CORNERS, OR WINGS.` · `SCATTERED THREADS, ONE HAND.` · then, large: `GATHER THE CORNERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold four threads together. Settle, and breathe. If you have a tallit, gather its fringes. If not, take four of anything: four strands of a scarf, four fingers of one hand curled into your palm, or simply four people. Name four people who are scattered from you: in another city, another country, out of touch. One for each corner. As you name each one, gather them into your hand. Then hold the bundle against your chest, and breathe with them there. The bell holds the time.
Tallit. The prayer shawl, with fringes on its four corners, gathered into one hand before the Shema.
Your line: gather the corners. Today, reach out to one of the four people you named, and bring them a little closer. Day five hundred sixty-five.

original.note: Hebrew: a prayer shawl, a four-cornered garment with tzitzit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious scarf.
what it means: a four-cornered garment whose fringes are gathered while the prayer asks for a scattered people to be gathered.
what a scholar hears: the gathering at me'arba kanfot ha'aretz echoes Isaiah 11:12; tzitzit are commanded in Numbers 15:38 and Deuteronomy 22:12, and Menachot 43a treats them as a daytime obligation.

sources.quoted: Thou shalt make thee twisted cords upon the four corners of thy covering, wherewith thou coverest thyself.

notes: Deuteronomy 22:12 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Custom of gathering tzitzit at vahavi'enu leshalom me'arba kanfot ha'aretz and holding them in the left hand (by the heart) through the Shema; kissing at each mention of tzitzit; confirm as widespread custom.
Who wears a tallit: Orthodox men (many Ashkenazim from marriage; many Sephardim from youth); many women in Conservative and Reform communities. Confirm fairness.
Menachot 43a: tzitzit as a time-bound (daytime) mitzvah; confirm.
